LeanInfoTheory.Shannon.indepProd: The independent product of probability laws p and q is the joint distribution obtained by drawing one sample from each law independently.
LeanInfoTheory.Shannon.indepProd_apply: Under the independent product of p and q, the probability of the pair (a,b) is p(a)q(b).
LeanInfoTheory.Shannon.indepProd_apply_e: The independent product of p and q gives (a,b) probability zero exactly when p(a) = 0 or q(b) = 0.
LeanInfoTheory.Shannon.indepProd_apply_n: The pair (a,b) has positive probability under the independent product of p and q exactly when both p(a) and q(b) are positive.
LeanInfoTheory.Shannon.support_indepProd: The support of the independent product of p and q is the Cartesian product of the support of p with the support of q.
LeanInfoTheory.Shannon.fstMarginal_indep: The first marginal of the independent product of p and q is p.
LeanInfoTheory.Shannon.sndMarginal_indep: The second marginal of the independent product of p and q is q.
LeanInfoTheory.Shannon.indepProd_map_swa: Swapping the two coordinates of the independent product p ⊗ q gives the independent product q ⊗ p.
LeanInfoTheory.Shannon.indepProd_toMeasu: For measurable sets S and T, the independent product of p and q assigns to the rectangle S × T the probability p(S)q(T).
The measure induced by the independent product of two probability mass functions equals the product of the measures induced by its factors.
LeanInfoTheory.Shannon.joint_toMeasure_a: For any joint law p on two finite alphabets, the induced measure of p is absolutely continuous with respect to the measure induced by the independent product of its two marginals.
On the product measurable space of two finite alphabets, the measure of any joint law is absolutely continuous with respect to the product of its marginal measures.
